questions.q: Why does this lesson say classifying a system by its kind matters more, at first, than knowing its vendor name?
options: Vendor names are irrelevant and never matter at any point in the architecture process
The kind of system (ERP, HCM, data warehouse, middleware, etc.) tells you far more about how to integrate with it than the brand name does
Vendor names are only relevant for legal contracts, never for architecture
All systems of the same vendor behave identically regardless of what kind of system they are
questions.explain: The lesson's point is that a system's category predicts its typical role and integration characteristics far better than its brand name does — knowing it's 'an ERP' tells you more up front than knowing it's 'SAP' or 'NetSuite' specifically.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what does an HCM/HRIS system typically serve as the system of record for?
options: The employee master — who's employed, their role, reporting line, and compensation band
Customer purchase history
Marketing campaign execution
Financial general ledger transactions
questions.explain: The lesson identifies HCM/HRIS systems as typically owning the employee master, with Salesforce often consuming a read-only feed from it for territory and approval hierarchies.

questions.q: A legacy mainframe system has no modern API and only produces a nightly flat-file export. What does this lesson say about proposing a real-time, bidirectional, event-driven integration against it?
options: It's always achievable with enough developer effort, regardless of the source system's actual capabilities
It's the recommended default for every legacy system, since real-time integration is always best
It's an aspirational design that will fail in production, because the architecture has to be honest about what the source system can actually support
Legacy systems should be ignored entirely and excluded from any integration design
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that proposing real-time, bidirectional integration against a system that can only produce a nightly batch export isn't aspirational, it's a design doomed to fail — the architecture must match what the system can actually do.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed among the key questions this lesson says a System Architect needs answered before designing any integration with an external system?
options: What color is the system's login screen?
How many employees work at the vendor company that built the system?
What programming language was the system originally written in?
Who owns the system, and what is its release cadence?
questions.explain: The lesson's list of key questions includes system-of-record status, actual API capability, ownership and release cadence, availability/performance, and whether the system is already scheduled for retirement.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say it matters whether a system is already scheduled for retirement before designing deep integration against it?
options: Deep integration work against a system already scheduled for decommissioning is largely wasted architecture effort
Retirement status has no bearing on integration design decisions
Scheduled retirement always means the integration should be rushed to completion before the deadline
Only systems scheduled for retirement are worth integrating with at all
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls out that building deep integration against a system already scheduled for decommissioning next year is wasted effort — checking retirement plans before investing architecture work is one of the key up-front questions.
